approachQuestion.prompt:
Balance two meters

A deterministic function f on [0,1] is strictly increasing and continuous, f(0)<0 and f(1)>0. Each evaluation is constant time. Given 0<epsilon<1/2, return a point within epsilon of its unique zero. Use an ideal exact-real arithmetic model. Examples: f(t)=t-0.3, epsilon=0.01 permits 0.296875; f(t)=2*t-1, epsilon=0.01 permits 0.5. Prefer worst-case evaluation count, then memory.
constraints: Use only the stated input ordering and access guarantees.

options.text: Maintain opposite-sign endpoints. Evaluate their midpoint; return on exact zero, otherwise replace the endpoint with the same sign. Once width <=2*epsilon, return the midpoint.
options.feedback: A function-value residual does not bound position error without a slope bound; bracket width does.

options.text: Store all evaluated points and signs in a list while applying the same interval updates.
options.feedback: The bracket is correct but retaining the entire trace adds avoidable memory.

options.text: Stop when abs(f(midpoint)) <= epsilon and return that midpoint, without bounding interval width.
options.feedback: For f(t)=0.001*(t-0.9), epsilon=0.01, midpoint 0.5 passes this test but is 0.4 from the zero.

feedback.reason: Maintain opposite-sign endpoints. Evaluate their midpoint; return on exact zero, otherwise replace the endpoint with the same sign. Once width <=2*epsilon, return the midpoint. A function-value residual does not bound position error without a slope bound; bracket width does.
details: Maintain opposite-sign endpoints. Evaluate their midpoint; return on exact zero, otherwise replace the endpoint with the same sign. Once width <=2*epsilon, return the midpoint. A function-value residual does not bound position error without a slope bound; bracket width does.

Opposite endpoint signs preserve a root-containing bracket by the stated continuity assumption. Width at most 2*epsilon makes its midpoint at most epsilon from every bracketed root. A small residual alone gives no positional guarantee without a slope bound.

“Maintain opposite-sign endpoints. Evaluate their midpoint; return on exact zero, otherwise replace the endpoint with the same sign. Once width <=2*epsilon, return the midpoint.”: A function-value residual does not bound position error without a slope bound; bracket width does.
“Store all evaluated points and signs in a list while applying the same interval updates.”: The bracket is correct but retaining the entire trace adds avoidable memory.
“Stop when abs(f(midpoint)) <= epsilon and return that midpoint, without bounding interval width.”: For f(t)=0.001*(t-0.9), epsilon=0.01, midpoint 0.5 passes this test but is 0.4 from the zero.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For target-method, choose the tightest worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair. Analyze only the bracket-width method under the ideal exact-real model explicitly given, not floating-point hardware. Each evaluation and arithmetic operation is constant time, with no trace or recursion. Input storage and returned result storage are excluded; all temporary buffers and call stacks are included.
constraints: Use worst-case bounds. Count all working memory including any stack; exclude supplied inputs and the scalar result.

feedback.reason: Each bisection halves bracket width under the stated exact-real cost model.
details: After t bisections the initial bracket width is divided by 2^t. Under the stated initial-width and exact-real assumptions, width<=2*epsilon takes O(log(1/epsilon)) iterations. Reuse endpoints and function values rather than storing the sequence of brackets.
“O(log(1/epsilon)) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: A function-value residual does not bound position error without a slope bound; bracket width does.
“O(log(1/epsilon)) time, O(log(1/epsilon) + 1) auxiliary space”: Iteration reuses two endpoints and their function values; it does not store an epsilon-dependent trace or recursion stack.
“O(1) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Arbitrarily small legal epsilon requires more width halvings even though each evaluation is constant time.
